summary: For strix's "local model as brain" architecture, the choice is really between Ollama and llama.cpp's own server, with vLLM as the high-end GPU option. Ollama is the best default: it is MIT-licensed, fully local/offline, needs no API key, ships an official typed Go client (github.com/ollama/ollama/api), and is itself a Go server wrapping llama.cpp. It supports OpenAI-style tool/function calling AND structured outputs, where a supplied JSON schema is compiled to a GBNF grammar and enforced token-by-token by llama.cpp's sampler — exactly the "the model cannot emit invalid tool calls" guarantee strix wants behind its deterministic Scope Guard. It runs CPU-only or GPU, uses GGUF, has tiny operational overhead (single daemon, simple model pull), and is the most "vibe-coding-friendly" to drive incrementally. llama.cpp/server is the power-user alternative giving direct GBNF and the latest tool-calling features (drive it over its OpenAI-compatible HTTP API with --jinja); it can even be embedded/static-linked if strix later wants a true single binary. vLLM is the choice only when a GPU server is available and high throughput matters (best-in-class guided decoding via xgrammar/outlines, but Python/heavy, not a fit for an air-gapped laptop). LM Studio is excellent UX and now free for commercial use, but it is proprietary/closed-source — acceptable as an operator-chosen backend over its OpenAI-compatible endpoint, but not something to bundle or depend on. llamafile (single-file, Apache/MIT, great for distributing a preloaded model) and KoboldCpp (GGUF, GBNF, OpenAI structured outputs) are solid secondary OSS options; GPT4All and text-generation-webui are usable via OpenAI-compatible endpoints but offer no advantage over Ollama/llama.cpp for agentic Go integration. Crucially, all OSS options here speak an OpenAI-compatible HTTP API, so strix should code to that interface and treat the runtime as swappable, defaulting to Ollama.

recommendations.name: Ollama
recommendations.why: Best default for strix. MIT-licensed Go server that wraps llama.cpp; offers an OFFICIAL, fully-typed Go client (github.com/ollama/ollama/api) with native ToolCalls support, plus an OpenAI-compatible /v1 endpoint. Supports tool/function calling and structured outputs: a JSON schema you pass is compiled into a GBNF grammar and grammar-constrained at the sampler, so invalid tool-call JSON is impossible at the token level — ideal upstream of the deterministic Scope Guard. CPU-only or GPU, GGUF models, trivial model management (ollama pull/run), single daemon. Lowest friction to vibe-code against. Tradeoff: thin abstraction means latest llama.cpp tool-calling/template tweaks land slightly later, and you depend on a background daemon rather than an in-process library.
recommendations.integration: go-lib (official github.com/ollama/ollama/api) + HTTP/RPC (native /api and OpenAI-compatible /v1); strix already uses it
recommendations.maturity: Very mature, dominant local-LLM runtime in 2025-2026, extremely active

recommendations.name: llama.cpp (+ server, llama-server)
recommendations.why: Power-user alternative and the engine under Ollama/llamafile/Kobold/LM Studio. MIT. Direct, first-class GBNF grammar + JSON-schema constrained decoding and the most up-to-date tool-calling: OpenAI-compatible /v1/chat/completions with `tools` when launched with --jinja, native templates for Llama 3.x, Qwen2.5/3, Hermes, Mistral-Nemo, Functionary, plus a generic fallback. Inspect /props for chat_template_tool_use to confirm a model supports tools. CPU/GPU, GGUF. Can be static-linked/embedded if strix later wants one binary. Tradeoffs: you manage the binary/model/templates yourself (no official Go client — drive via HTTP), generic templates are token-heavy, and aggressive KV-cache quant (e.g. q4_0) degrades tool-calling.
recommendations.integration: shell-out CLI (launch llama-server) + HTTP (OpenAI-compatible /v1); optional embed/cgo for single static binary
recommendations.maturity: Extremely mature and the most actively developed local inference engine

recommendations.name: vLLM
recommendations.why: High-throughput GPU alternative for when an operator has a real GPU box and wants batched/concurrent inference (e.g. parallel recon agents). Best-in-class structured output: guided_json/guided_regex/guided_choice/guided_grammar via xgrammar, outlines, or lm-format-enforcer (auto-selected), plus OpenAI-compatible tool calling. Apache-2.0, fully local, no API key. Tradeoffs: Python, heavy GPU/VRAM requirements, non-trivial to deploy, and a poor fit for an air-gapped single-laptop/CPU operator — overkill for strix's default profile.
recommendations.integration: HTTP (OpenAI-compatible server) — strix shells out to / connects to it
recommendations.maturity: Mature, production-grade, very active; the standard for self-hosted GPU serving

recommendations.name: llamafile
recommendations.why: Best option for distributing a preloaded model as one self-contained artifact (Cosmopolitan Libc -> single cross-platform executable bundling weights+engine+server). OSS (Apache-2.0 project incl. llama.cpp MIT), runs offline, OpenAI-compatible /v1 in server mode, GGUF, CPU-first. Great if strix wants a 'download one file, get the brain' onboarding. Tradeoffs: tracks llama.cpp slightly behind; tool-calling/grammar feature parity depends on the bundled llama.cpp version; less convenient for swapping many models than Ollama.
recommendations.integration: shell-out CLI (run the .llamafile in --server mode) + HTTP OpenAI-compatible /v1
recommendations.maturity: Maintained by Mozilla.ai; active but smaller cadence than llama.cpp/Ollama

recommendations.name: KoboldCpp
recommendations.why: Solid single-binary OSS alternative (AGPL). One file, zero install, GGUF, CPU/GPU. Supports GBNF grammar sampling and added OpenAI Structured Outputs in its /v1 chat completions (accepts a JSON schema, including via the `grammar` field). Good fallback runtime an operator may already use. Tradeoffs: AGPL-3.0 is copyleft — fine for shelling out to a separate process over HTTP, but do NOT link/embed it into strix's binary; its tool-calling story is less standardized than llama.cpp/Ollama.
recommendations.integration: shell-out CLI + HTTP OpenAI-compatible /v1 (keep as a separate process to respect AGPL)
recommendations.maturity: Mature, actively maintained, popular in local/hobbyist scene

recommendations.name: LM Studio
recommendations.why: Best polished desktop UX and now free for personal AND commercial use; OpenAI-compatible /v1 (and /v1/responses) with tool calling and JSON-schema structured output, GGUF + MLX, CPU/GPU. Reasonable as an operator-selected backend strix talks to over HTTP. Tradeoff (important): PROPRIETARY / closed-source. It violates the spirit of strix being a free OSS stack if bundled or hard-depended-on; treat strictly as an optional, user-supplied endpoint, never a default or embedded component.
recommendations.license: Proprietary (free for personal + commercial; CLI `lms` is MIT)
recommendations.integration: HTTP only (OpenAI-compatible /v1) — optional operator-chosen backend, do not bundle
recommendations.maturity: Mature, very popular, actively released through 2025-2026

recommendations.name: GPT4All
recommendations.why: Easy desktop app with a localhost OpenAI-compatible server (port 4891), Apache-2.0, GGUF, CPU-friendly, commercial-use OK. Workable as a swappable backend. Tradeoffs: implements only a SUBSET of the OpenAI API, weaker/less-documented tool-calling and grammar story than Ollama/llama.cpp, localhost-only by design — no real advantage for strix's agentic loop, so list as a minor alternative.
recommendations.maturity: Maintained by Nomic; active but less central for agentic use in 2026

recommendations.name: text-generation-webui (oobabooga)
recommendations.why: Flexible multi-backend UI with an OpenAI/Anthropic-compatible API including tool-calling and SSE streaming; AGPL-3.0, fully local, supports GGUF (via llama.cpp loader) and other formats. Usable if an operator already runs it. Tradeoffs: heavier Python stack, AGPL copyleft (run as separate process only), and offers nothing strix needs beyond what Ollama/llama.cpp provide more simply — keep as a last-resort alternative.
recommendations.integration: shell-out / separate process + HTTP OpenAI-compatible API (respect AGPL)
recommendations.maturity: Actively maintained into 2026, but niche for headless agentic Go use

pitfalls: Tool-calling reliability depends heavily on the MODEL + its chat template, not just the runtime. Use a model with a native tool-use template (Qwen2.5/Qwen3, Llama 3.1/3.3, Hermes 3, Functionary, Mistral-Nemo). Generic/fallback templates consume more tokens and are less reliable.

Structured-output (JSON-schema/GBNF) constraint and tool-call constraint are different paths: schema-based structured output is grammar-enforced at the sampler (cannot produce invalid JSON), but OpenAI-style `tools` calls inject the schema into the prompt and are NOT always fully grammar-constrained — validate/parse tool-call args defensively in Go and reject on parse failure (strix's Scope Guard must never trust model output structurally).
Aggressive KV-cache quantization (e.g. -ctk q4_0) in llama.cpp can substantially DEGRADE tool-calling quality — keep KV cache at higher precision for the planning model.

llama.cpp server needs --jinja for OpenAI tool calling; without the right template flags, `tools` requests silently fall back or fail. Check /props (chat_template_tool_use) to confirm support per model.

License traps for a bundled OSS product: LM Studio is PROPRIETARY (never embed/bundle); KoboldCpp and text-generation-webui are AGPL-3.0 (only safe via separate-process HTTP, never linked into strix's binary). Ollama (MIT), llama.cpp (MIT), llamafile (Apache/MIT), vLLM (Apache-2.0), GPT4All (MIT/Apache) are safe to depend on.

Ollama tracks llama.cpp with a lag, so brand-new tool-calling/template fixes (and some new model formats) may land in llama.cpp/server first — if a specific 2026 model's tool calling is broken in Ollama, llama-server is the escape hatch.

Don't hard-couple strix to one runtime's native API. Every OSS option here exposes an OpenAI-compatible /v1 endpoint; code to that interface (with the official Ollama Go client as the optimized default path) so operators can swap runtimes.

CPU-only inference of a capable agentic model (7B-30B) is slow; manage operator expectations or recommend small fast models (e.g. Qwen3/Hermes 3 8B at Q4_K_M) for laptop/air-gapped use, larger MoE models (Qwen3-Coder-30B-A3B) where RAM/VRAM allows.
open_questions: Default deployment profile: is strix's primary target a CPU-only/air-gapped laptop (favors Ollama or a bundled llamafile) or an operator with a GPU (could optionally support vLLM for parallel agents)?

Single-binary vision vs. daemon dependency: does strix want to embed/static-link an engine (llama.cpp via cgo, or bundle a llamafile) for true single-binary distribution, or is requiring the operator to run Ollama acceptable?
Should strix abstract behind the OpenAI-compatible /v1 interface for runtime-swappability, while keeping the native Ollama Go client as the optimized default? (Recommended yes.)
Which default model ships/recommended with strix, and at what quant — this drives tool-calling reliability more than the runtime choice (e.g. Qwen3 / Hermes 3 8B vs Qwen3-Coder-30B-A3B MoE)?
Is shelling out to AGPL tools (KoboldCpp/oobabooga) as optional operator-provided backends acceptable to the project's licensing posture, given they'd be separate processes (not linked)?
Does strix need batched/concurrent inference for many simultaneous agents (which would justify a vLLM backend path), or is a single sequential planning loop sufficient?
